Source: https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/network.md

# Laravel Cloud Network

Learn how Laravel Cloud networking works, including edge security, caching, WAF, rate limiting, and custom network settings.

## IntroductionLaravel Cloud manages all aspects of networking for every application.
Cloud's networking infrastructure has two main layers: the Cloud Edge Network and the Cloud Compute Network.> [!NOTE]
>
> Private Cloud customers with a dedicated edge network have access to additional networking features including custom rules, cache rules, and private connections to AWS resources. See [Dedicated edge network](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/private-cloud/edge-network) and [Private networking](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/private-cloud/private-networking) in the Private Cloud documentation.## Cloud edge networkLaravel Cloud has partnered with [Cloudflare](https://cloudflare.com) to offer every application globally distributed caching and network security at the edge.Each incoming HTTP request first goes to the nearest edge region, out of 335 cities around the world, and passes through DDoS mitigation and Web Application Firewall (WAF) security layers. The edge then returns the response from the cache, if available. Otherwise, it passes the request on to the Cloud Compute Network, which routes it to your application's compute cluster.### Cache controlAn important job of the Cloud Edge Network is caching your application's static assets. Caching reduces the number of requests that your application's compute needs to handle, and it decreases latency for your users.Laravel Cloud manages your CDN cache in two steps. First, Cloud uses a long cache lifespan so the edge serves your static assets as often as possible. Second, Cloud clears the CDN cache automatically on every deployment so no stale files remain in the cache.By default, Laravel Cloud caches files with the following extensions:`7Z`, `APK`, `AVI`, `AVIF`, `BIN`, `BMP`, `BZ2`, `CLASS`, `CSS`, `CSV`, `DMG`, `DOC`, `DOCX`, `EJS`, `EOT`, `EPS`, `EXE`, `FLAC`, `GIF`, `GZ`, `ICO`, `ISO`, `JAR`, `JPEG`, `JPG`, `JS`, `MID`, `MIDI`, `MKV`, `MP3`, `MP4`, `OGG`, `OTF`, `PDF`, `PICT`, `PLS`, `PNG`, `PPT`, `PPTX`, `PS`, `RAR`, `SVG`, `SVGZ`, `SWF`, `TAR`, `TIF`, `TIFF`, `TTF`, `WEBM`, `WEBP`, `WOFF`, `WOFF2`, `XLS`, `XLSX`, `ZIP`, `ZST`If your application does not set a `Cache-Control` directive or `Expires` header, Laravel Cloud uses the HTTP status code to determine the cache duration.| HTTP status code | Default TTL |
| - | - |
| 200, 206, 301 | 120m |
| 302, 303 | 20m |
| 404, 410 | 3m |By default, Laravel Cloud does not cache responses with any other status code.You may override the default cache rules by setting your own `Cache-Control` and `Expires` headers in your application code. Laravel Cloud respects these headers and caches your assets according to the rules you set.Certain headers set by your application can prevent Laravel Cloud from caching a response:- The `Set-Cookie` header prevents caching.
- The `Authorization` header prevents caching, unless a `must-revalidate`, `public`, or `s-maxage` header is also present.To reduce the risk of the cache serving stale files, Laravel Cloud enables the **Purge edge cache on deploy** setting for your environment by default. To disable this setting, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas. From there, you can also purge the cache manually or bypass the cache entirely.> [!WARNING]
>
> Bypassing the cache sends all requests to your application, which may increase latency and load on your compute cluster.
> We don't recommend bypassing the cache unless you are debugging a specific issue.### Response rulesLaravel Cloud lets you configure security headers that it sets on every response. To modify the defaults, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas and select the option you want. You can also override the default headers by setting them directly in your application code.#### X-Frame-OptionsBy default, Laravel Cloud sets an `X-Frame-Options: DENY` header. The header prevents certain types of attacks that can occur when an application is loaded in an iframe. If your application needs to allow iframes, click **Edge network** on the environment's canvas and change the header value to `SAMEORIGIN` or unset it entirely.#### X-Content-Type-OptionsBy default, Laravel Cloud sets an `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` header. The header stops browsers from interpreting files as a different MIME type than the one the `Content-Type` header specifies. Blocking that reinterpretation stops attacks based on MIME-type confusion.
If your application needs browsers to interpret files as a different MIME type, click **Edge network** on the environment's canvas and select **None** to unset the header entirely.> [!NOTE]
>
> If you select the **None** option for the `X-Content-Type-Options` header, your application can override the default and set a `nosniff` value at the route level. However, the opposite is not true. If you select the `nosniff` option, your application cannot unset the value.#### Strict-Transport-SecurityHSTS is disabled by default, and you can enable it with a toggle. When HSTS is enabled, Laravel Cloud sets a `Strict-Transport-Security` header with a max-age of 31536000 seconds (1 year). You can customize the max-age. The header enforces secure (HTTPS) connections to the server.You can also enable the `includeSubDomains` and `preload` directives. The `includeSubDomains` directive applies the HSTS policy to all subdomains of your application. The `preload` directive allows browsers to include your domain in their HSTS preload lists, so browsers enforce HTTPS for your domain and its subdomains even before the first request. Before you enable these directives, make sure you understand their implications. Browsers cache them, so they can be difficult to remove once set.#### Markdown for AgentsMarkdown for Agents converts HTML to Markdown in real time at the edge for AI agents and crawlers. When the setting is enabled, AI systems can request your application's pages in Markdown format by including `Accept: text/markdown` in their request headers. Cloudflare's network converts the HTML response to Markdown before serving it to the client.AI systems understand Markdown's explicit structure better than raw HTML, and Markdown uses far fewer tokens. When Cloudflare converts a response, it includes the following headers:- **`x-markdown-tokens`**: An estimated token count of the Markdown document, useful for calculating context window sizes or chunking strategies.
- **`content-signal`**: Indicates AI usage permissions following the [Content Signals](https://contentsignals.org/) framework. The default value is `ai-train=yes, search=yes, ai-input=yes`.To enable or disable Markdown for Agents, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas and toggle the setting in the **Response** section.> [!NOTE]
>
> The origin response must not exceed 2 MB, and only HTML content is eligible for conversion. For more information, refer to [Cloudflare's Markdown for Agents documentation](https://developers.cloudflare.com/fundamentals/reference/markdown-for-agents/).### X-Robots-TagTeams often use Laravel Cloud domains for testing and staging, so Laravel Cloud sets an `X-Robots-Tag: noindex, nofollow` header on all `*.laravel.cloud` domains to keep search engines from indexing them. To remove this header, configure a custom domain for your application. Laravel Cloud does not set the header on custom domains.## Cloud compute networkLaravel Cloud routes requests that your application needs to process to the Compute Network in the AWS region assigned to your Laravel Cloud application.The Cloud Compute Network is built for security and scale. Your applications run in private networks, and the public can reach them only through the Cloud Edge Network.
Laravel Cloud distributes compute clusters across multiple availability zones (AZs), so a region stays stable and recovers quickly if a single zone has an interruption.The Compute Network also load balances traffic across all instances in your compute cluster as you scale horizontally up or down.## Web application firewallThe Web Application Firewall (WAF) provides advanced protection for your Laravel Cloud applications by filtering and monitoring HTTP traffic between your application and the Internet.All traffic routed through Laravel Cloud's edge network, via the default `app.laravel.cloud` hostname or a custom domain proxied through Cloudflare, runs behind Cloudflare's [OWASP Core Ruleset](https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/managed-rules/reference/owasp-core-ruleset/). The ruleset gives every environment managed protection that maps to the OWASP Top 10 before traffic reaches your app.> [!NOTE]
>
> Cloudflare's managed rules can flag server-to-server callbacks that use a default library `User-Agent` (for example, Python's `urllib`). If you're migrating from a platform that didn't sit behind Cloudflare (for example, Laravel Vapor, which fronts applications with CloudFront) and an inbound webhook starts failing with no application-level error, set a descriptive `User-Agent` header on the sending request rather than relying on the library default.### Bot categoriesBot categories let you present a JavaScript challenge to clients identified as specific types of automated traffic. Visitors matching your selected bot categories see a challenge before they can access your application. Categories include, but are not limited to, AI crawlers, AI assistants, advertising and marketing bots, aggregators, search engine optimization bots, social media marketing bots, and monitoring tools.To configure bot categories, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas and select the **Firewall** tab.> [!NOTE]
>
> Bot categories are available for [Business plan](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/pricing) customers.### Rate limitingRate limiting protects your application from abuse by controlling how many requests a client can make within a given time period.#### Basic rate limitingWhen basic rate limiting is enabled, Laravel Cloud intercepts requests from any IP address that exceeds 100 requests per minute.You can choose from three actions:- **Challenge**: Present a challenge (CAPTCHA or Turnstile) to the IP address. Laravel Cloud shows the challenge for 5 minutes.
- **Throttle**: Block new requests from the IP address for 5 minutes.
- **Ban**: Block all requests from the IP address for 5 minutes.To configure basic rate limiting, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas and select the **Firewall** tab.> [!NOTE]
>
> Basic rate limiting is available for [Growth and Business plan](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/pricing) customers.#### Advanced rate limitingAdvanced rate limiting includes all basic rate limiting features plus additional customization:- **Customizable threshold**: Set your own requests per minute threshold instead of the default 100 rpm.
- **Block repeated 4xx responses**: Block clients that send more than 30 unauthorized or error requests (401, 403, 404) per minute. The block lasts 10 minutes.
- **Block excess 429 responses**: Block clients that continue sending traffic after receiving more than 5 rate limit responses from your application. The block lasts 10 minutes.> [!NOTE]
>
> Advanced rate limiting is available for [Business plan](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/pricing) customers.### Path blockingPath blocking stops requests to common vulnerability paths at the edge, returning a `404` response before the request reaches your application. Because blocked requests never reach your compute, scanners probing these paths cannot wake an environment that has scaled to zero.Path blocking blocks requests for the following file extensions and paths:- **Extensions**: `.php`, `.php3`, `.php4`, `.php5`, `.php6`, `.php7`, `.php8`, `.phtml`, `.pht`, `.phps`, `.env`, and `.git`
- **Paths**: `/wp-admin`, `/wp-content`, `/wp-includes`, and `/wp-json`Path blocking is enabled by default for new environments. To enable or disable it, click the **Edge network** card on your environment's canvas and select the **Firewall** tab. You cannot customize the list of blocked extensions and paths.### Under attack modeIf your application is experiencing a large-scale attack or suspicious traffic spikes, you can enable **Under Attack Mode** in the edge network settings for your environment. When Under Attack Mode is active:* All incoming traffic to your environment is filtered through additional Cloudflare security checks designed to mitigate layer 7 DDoS attacks.
* Visitors see an interstitial "Checking your browser before accessing..." page and must pass a JavaScript challenge, which typically takes no more than 5 seconds.
* Cloudflare lets validated users through and blocks suspicious or automated traffic.
* Under Attack Mode is intended as a last resort during active threats and may temporarily pause access to your site and impact your site analytics.
* Under Attack Mode expires automatically after 24 hours, so normal access returns.
* Browsers must support JavaScript to pass the challenge. Some third-party analytics tools may be affected.> [!WARNING]
>
> The additional security checks in Under Attack Mode may temporarily affect the experience of legitimate visitors. Use this mode only when necessary.## IP addressesLaravel Cloud applications may make outbound requests from any of the following IP addresses. Use these addresses when you configure firewalls, security groups, or allowlists for external services that your application needs to access.> [!WARNING]
>
> If your organization has dedicated compute available from [Private Cloud](https://laravel.com/cloud/docs/private-cloud), make sure to use the dedicated IP addresses provided during your onboarding instead of the ranges listed on this page.

### Programmatic accessThe IP addresses are also available through the API:```bash theme={null}
curl https://laravel.com/api/ip
```This endpoint returns a JSON object with IP addresses organized by region:```json theme={null}
{
  "us-east-2": {
    "ipv4": ["3.140.62.214", "3.139.253.68", ...],
    "ipv6": ["2600:1f16:e0:8500::/56"]
  },
  "eu-west-2": {
    "ipv4": ["35.178.113.65", ...],
    "ipv6": ["2a05:d01c:243:e500::/56"]
  }
}
```> [!NOTE]
>
> These IP addresses may change. We recommend checking this endpoint regularly or subscribing to our changelog for updates.
